Specifically, Article 234(2)(a)(i) and 234(2)(j) of the Constitution provide that the Public Service Commission has the exclusive authority to establish and abolish offices in the public service, with the exception of the President. Any attempt by a State Corporation to perform these functions independently would contravene this constitutional provision.

This invalidity is further supported by the findings in the case Law Society of Kenya v Attorney General (Sued on Behalf of the President of Kenya) 6 others Katiba Institute (Interested Party) (Petition E273of2024) 2025KEHC15858(KLR) (Constitutional and Human Rights) (7November2025) (Judgment), where it was held that the regulation of the human resource of state corporations falls squarely under the constitutional mandate of the Public Service Commission. Therefore, any action by a State Corporation to establish or abolish offices without the Public Service Commission's involvement would be unconstitutional and unlawful. The judge further clarified that the phrase "sufficient reason" does not necessarily have to be analogous or ejusdem generis to the other reasons stipulated in Order 45 Rule 1. In such cases, the court has the discretion to deal with the matter if the justice of the case so requires, and the appropriate remedy is to remit the matter for fresh taxation before a different taxing officer [chunk_id: Mwangi ta Raydon Mwangi  Associates Advocates v Njenga (Miscellaneous Application E025of2024) 2026KEHC13078(KLR) (13August2026) (Ruling)__s3__c12].

expected_value: The court must consider that an extension of time is an equitable remedy rather than a right, that the applicant bears the burden of laying a satisfactory basis for the delay, and that it must assess whether the respondents will suffer prejudice if the extension is granted.
answer:
According to the Supreme Court's guidelines in Nicholas Kiptoo Arap Korir Salat v Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission & 7 others (2014) eKLR, the court must consider the following factors when exercising its discretion to grant an extension of time:

1. Extension of time is not a right of a party. It is an equitable remedy that is only available to a deserving party at the discretion of the court.
2. A party who seeks for extension of time has the burden of laying a basis to the satisfaction of the court.
3. Whether the court should exercise the discretion to extend time, is a consideration to be made on a case to case basis.
4. Whether there is a reasonable reason for the delay. The delay should be explained to the satisfaction of the court.
5. Whether there will be any prejudice suffered by the respondents if the extension is granted.
6. Whether the application has been brought without undue delay.
7. Whether in certain cases, like election petitions, public interest should be a consideration for extending time. [chunk_id: Ruto v Maru (Miscellaneous Civil Application E001of2023) 2024KEHC2378(KLR) (8March2024) (Ruling)__s2__c12]
correctness_reasoning: The answer correctly states that extension of time is an equitable remedy, that the applicant bears the burden of justifying the delay, and that the court must consider prejudice to the respondents, which matches the reference.
faithfulness_reasoning: The answer is fully supported by the provided context and accurately reproduces the Supreme Court’s listed factors, including the equitable nature of the remedy, the applicant’s burden to justify the request, and prejudice to the respondent.
